props.title: The Killer That Stalked New York

sections.content: The Killer That Stalked New York (1950) stands as a remarkable fusion of film noir and public health thriller, arriving during noir's golden age. Director Earl McEvoy crafted this taut narrative based on the real 1947 smallpox outbreak in New York City, predating similar disease outbreak films like Panic in the Streets (1950). The film's stark black-and-white cinematography by Joseph Biroc transforms New York City into a maze of threatening shadows and cramped spaces, mirroring similar urban anxiety found in The Naked City (1948) and Call Northside 777 (1948).

sections.content: The film's star Evelyn Keyes delivers a complex performance as diamond smuggler Sheila Bennett, who unknowingly carries smallpox while evading police. This dual threat - criminal and carrier - creates a unique noir atmosphere where the femme fatale becomes both villain and victim. The film's documentary-style approach to showing public health response predates later outbreak films like The Andromeda Strain (1971) and Outbreak (1995), while maintaining noir's signature moral ambiguity.

What sets The Killer That Stalked New York apart is its brilliant fusion of two distinct 1950s film trends: noir's focus on urban crime and post-war America's growing obsession with public health threats. Similar themes would later emerge in Panic in the Streets (1950) and The Whip Hand (1951), but McEvoy's film uniquely captures both the procedural aspects of disease control and the psychological tension of noir. SUBHEAD: Public Health Meets Film Noir

movies.slug: Scientific thriller about a team of scientists racing to contain an deadly alien microorganism

sections.content: The film's depiction of New York City's public health infrastructure reveals fascinating historical detail while maintaining noir's signature style. Like D.O.A. (1950) and Kiss Me Deadly (1955), the film uses its thriller elements to explore deeper societal anxieties - in this case, the fear of invisible threats in the post-war urban landscape. The documentary-style sequences showing mass vaccinations and contact tracing feel remarkably contemporary, especially viewed through a post-COVID lens.
